red.focus: Distinguish a fast legal decision from a fair legal decision.
red.summary: Efficiency concerns how resources and time are used; fairness concerns how people are treated and which burdens they carry. Learn why the two can support each other yet sometimes point in different directions.
checklist: I can identify a procedural shortcut and its benefits
I can recognize who may bear the costs of speed
I can explain why an opportunity to be heard matters

sections.title: Speed can help a person in need
sections.body_md: A family waiting for a housing decision may suffer if a case takes years. A simpler form and an earlier hearing can help them obtain relief before an eviction becomes irreversible. Efficient procedure can therefore promote justice. But a rule that decides every application in one minute without hearing relevant evidence might make the system fast at the price of accuracy. The proper question is which resources are saved and whose rights or interests are affected by the shortcut.
sections.audio_script: A family waiting for a housing decision may suffer if a case takes years. But a rule that decides every application in one minute without hearing relevant evidence might make the system fast at the price of accuracy. The proper question is which resources are saved and whose rights or interests are affected by the shortcut.

sections.title: An equal rule can have unequal effects
sections.body_md: A filing fee of one hundred dollars looks identical for every person, but it may exclude a worker who lacks money while being trivial for a large business. Formal sameness does not establish equal practical access. A court may lawfully charge fees, but policymakers should examine waiver rules, legal assistance, and alternative procedures where authorized. The fairness question concerns who can use the system and whether decisions reflect the merits rather than unequal resources. Cost must be counted for the parties as well as the public.

sections.title: Find improvements that serve both values
sections.body_md: An online notice system could reduce administrative expense and reach many litigants quickly. It could also exclude people without reliable devices or accessible language support. A responsible design would preserve alternative notice methods and provide a way to correct missed communications. Efficiency is not simply the opposite of fairness; thoughtful administration can reduce unnecessary delay while protecting participation. Before praising a proposal, ask how it affects the poor, the unrepresented, and people facing urgent legal consequences.

yellow.focus: Apply cost-benefit reasoning without mistaking gains for justice.
yellow.summary: Cost-benefit analysis compares consequences, but it cannot decide whose interests should count or how benefits are distributed. Distinguish Pareto improvements from changes that help some while harming others.
checklist: I can explain why efficiency metrics need a specified objective
I can distinguish Pareto improvement from redistribution
I can evaluate the distributional impact of legal reforms

sections.title: Decide which costs are counted
sections.body_md: A rule limiting discovery may reduce legal fees and court time but also prevent claimants from obtaining records controlled by defendants. Measuring only court budgets would miss those private costs and the value of accurate decisions. A rigorous analysis identifies direct expenses, delay, expected error, enforcement costs, and harm to vulnerable persons. It should avoid counting time saved as a benefit without asking whether the time was previously used to protect a right. The baseline and affected population matter.
sections.audio_script: A rule limiting discovery may reduce legal fees and court time but also prevent claimants from obtaining records controlled by defendants. Measuring only court budgets would miss those private costs and the value of accurate decisions. A rigorous analysis identifies direct expenses, delay, expected error, enforcement costs, and harm to vulnerable persons. It should avoid counting time saved as a benefit without asking whether the time was previously used to protect a right. The baseline and affected population matter.

sections.title: Pareto improvement is a narrow idea
sections.body_md: A Pareto improvement makes at least one person better off without leaving anyone worse off, under the specified assessment. Many real legal reforms cannot meet that standard because litigation, taxation, and regulation redistribute burdens. A change may increase total welfare while harming a smaller group. It is a mistake to call any net benefit a Pareto improvement. Legal analysis must identify the losers and consider whether their rights, compensation, and opportunity to challenge the change receive proper regard.

sections.title: Respect procedures as well as outcomes
sections.body_md: A regulator may find that a policy saves more money than it costs, but its governing statute could require consultation, individual notice, or specific rights protections. Economic usefulness does not replace those conditions. A good proposal explains both how the policy works and why the responsible institution may lawfully implement it. The lawyer should separate the empirical prediction of net gains from normative judgments about acceptable sacrifice and the legally binding constraints on official action.

orange.focus: Contrast Rawlsian justice with economic efficiency and Coasian bargaining.
orange.summary: John Rawls emphasizes equal basic liberties, fair opportunity, and benefit to the least advantaged; economic analysis examines incentives and resource use. Test when bargaining and compensation can achieve good outcomes and when unequal power defeats them.
checklist: I can state the function of Rawls's difference principle accurately
I can identify assumptions behind Coasian bargaining
I can evaluate efficiency claims under unequal rights and bargaining power

sections.title: A just distribution is not simply a large total
sections.body_md: In A Theory of Justice, Rawls argued that principles chosen under fair conditions would secure equal basic liberties and fair equality of opportunity, with social and economic inequalities arranged to benefit the least advantaged. His difference principle is not the claim that every inequality is unjust. It supplies a distinct standard from maximizing total income. A legal reform that enriches most people while worsening the situation of those at the bottom requires scrutiny from a Rawlsian perspective even if its aggregate economic gains are high.
sections.audio_script: In A Theory of Justice, Rawls argued that principles chosen under fair conditions would secure equal basic liberties and fair equality of opportunity, with social and economic inequalities arranged to benefit the least advantaged. His difference principle is not the claim that every inequality is unjust. It supplies a distinct standard from maximizing total income. A legal reform that enriches most people while worsening the situation of those at the bottom requires scrutiny from a Rawlsian perspective even if its aggregate economic gains are high.

sections.title: Coase isolates the friction of bargaining
sections.body_md: Ronald Coase showed why transaction costs and the initial allocation of legal entitlements matter in conflicts involving external harms. Under restrictive idealized assumptions, including costless bargaining, parties might negotiate efficient allocations despite different initial rights. Real parties face information gaps, strategic behavior, unequal resources, and collective-action problems. The proposition does not say that legal rights are irrelevant or that bargaining always works. It highlights the need to examine the institutions and costs surrounding supposedly private deals.

The proposition does not say that legal rights are irrelevant or that bargaining always works. It highlights the need to examine the institutions and costs surrounding supposedly private deals.

sections.title: Justice and incentives can be combined carefully
sections.body_md: Imagine a factory emits smoke that harms nearby residents. A regulator may compare prevention costs, the value of production, and health effects, while law may protect residents from particular hazards regardless of a calculated net benefit. Compensation could help but may not restore lost health or equal bargaining power. An advanced lawyer identifies lawful entitlements, relevant incentives, who can negotiate, and what relief is enforceable. Good reasoning acknowledges efficiency without allowing the welfare of the most vulnerable to disappear into totals.

black.focus: Defend efficient institutions without sacrificing procedural equality or basic rights.
black.summary: Economic efficiency can improve legal capacity, but welfare metrics may value powerful preferences more heavily than vulnerable persons' needs. Build a theory of legal design that makes accuracy, rights, distribution, and public trust explicit.
checklist: I can critique willingness-to-pay as a measure of human benefit
I can compare consequentialist and rights-based institutional criteria
I can construct a measurable yet rights-respecting reform

sections.title: The welfare metric embodies assumptions
sections.body_md: Economic analysis sometimes evaluates policies by aggregate willingness to pay. Because the wealthy can pay more, this measure may reflect purchasing power as well as actual need. It can be useful for some resource decisions without settling whether a person's liberty or basic dignity may be sacrificed for benefits to others. A doctoral analysis distinguishes empirical estimates from the moral principle authorizing trade-offs. Rights can act as constraints rather than commodities traded against every possible increase in output.
sections.audio_script: Economic analysis sometimes evaluates policies by aggregate willingness to pay. Because the wealthy can pay more, this measure may reflect purchasing power as well as actual need. It can be useful for some resource decisions without settling whether a person's liberty or basic dignity may be sacrificed for benefits to others. A doctoral analysis distinguishes empirical estimates from the moral principle authorizing trade-offs. Rights can act as constraints rather than commodities traded against every possible increase in output.

sections.title: Fair process can create efficiency over time
sections.body_md: A person excluded from court may lose trust, ignore obligations, or face repeated harm that later requires costly intervention. An impartial hearing can identify errors early and improve public confidence, while uncontrolled procedural complexity can trap everyone in delay. Compare false dismissal and baseless litigation, short-term expense and long-term effects, and the distribution of each burden. A fair design need not demand maximal process in every case; it demands process proportionate to the consequences and legal rights involved.

A fair design need not demand maximal process in every case; it demands process proportionate to the consequences and legal rights involved.

sections.title: Propose and test a constrained reform
sections.body_md: Design a small-claims procedure with plain-language forms, accessible assistance, staged evidence exchange, prompt decisions, reasons for rejection, and a lawful correction route. Measure total cost, processing time, factual accuracy, and outcomes across income groups. Require the reform to satisfy constitutional and statutory rights rather than claiming favorable statistics authorize any shortcut. If evidence reveals that a faster method denies remedies disproportionately to unrepresented people, revise it. Legitimate efficiency is accountable improvement, not the concealment of whose rights were traded away.
